faqs.q: How do I convert an hourly rate to an annual salary for a business analyst role?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role, we assume 38 hours per week. For example, $50 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $98,800 per year. This is a gross figure before tax and super. faqs.q: Does the National Minimum Wage apply to business analysts in Melbourne?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage ($26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026) is the legal floor for award-free employees. Most business analysts are covered by an award such as the Professional Employees Award or the Clerks Award, which set higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides list the correct award rates. A business analyst salary in Melbourne is typically well above the minimum, but you should confirm your classification.

faqs.q: How is casual loading and superannuation calculated for a business analyst?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an additional 25% on top of the base hourly rate, intended to compensate for lack of leave entitlements. Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (from 1 July 2026) up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. For a casual business analyst earning $50 per hour, the casual rate would be $62.50 per hour, and super would be calculated on the $50 base (or the casual rate, depending on the award). bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Hourly to Annual Conversions

When you're evaluating a **business analyst salary in Melbourne**, the first step is often converting an hourly rate to an annual figure. The standard formula is simple: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For full-time employees, we assume a 38-hour week, which is the ordinary hours under many modern awards and the National Employment Standards.

For example, if you're offered $50 per hour as a business analyst, your annual gross pay would be:

$50 × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $98,800 per year.

This calculation assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. It's a starting point for comparing job offers or checking your current pay.

### The Fortnightly View

Many Australians are paid fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, multiply your weekly pay by two. Using the same $50 per hour example:

- Weekly: $50 × 38 = $1,900
- Fortnightly: $1,900 × 2 = $3,800

This can help you budget and compare with salary figures often quoted per annum.

## National Minimum Wage vs. Award Rates

The Fair Work Ombudsman sets the National Minimum Wage, which from 1 July 2026 is **$26.44 per hour** or **$1,004.90 per week** for 38 hours. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, making the minimum casual rate **$33.05 per hour**.

However, most business analysts are covered by a modern award. The Fair Work Commission's Modern Awards Pay Database provides detailed minimum rates, allowances, and penalty rates for each classification. For example, a business analyst might fall under the *Professional Employees Award* or the *Clerks – Private Sector Award*, depending on their duties and industry. These awards typically set higher minimum rates than the National Minimum Wage.

If you're unsure which award applies, use the Fair Work Ombudsman's [pay guides](/blog) or the [reference tables](/data) on this site.

## Business Analyst Salary in Melbourne: What the Data Shows

According to Glassdoor, the typical **business analyst salary in Melbourne** ranges from **$82,000 to $120,000 per year**, with an average of **$96,000** as of October 2026. This translates to roughly $41 to $61 per hour for a 38-hour week.

Keep in mind that Glassdoor data is based on user-submitted salaries and may not reflect official award rates or the Australian Bureau of Statistics' averages. The ABS reports that full-time adult average weekly ordinary time earnings were **$2,083.70 per week** (May 2026), which is about **$108,352 per year** for a 38-hour week. This is a broader measure across all occupations.

For a more precise estimate, check the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page or use the [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool on this site.

## Tax and Superannuation

Once you have your annual gross figure, you can estimate your take-home pay using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (generally). The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page can help you calculate after-tax income.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at **12%** (from 1 July 2026), up to the maximum contribution base of **$270,830**. For a business analyst earning $98,800 per year, the super contribution would be $11,856 per year, added to your salary package. Learn more about [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

### Casual Loading

If you work as a casual business analyst, you're entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. This compensates for not receiving paid leave. When using the [timesheet](/), you can check the "casual loading" box to see the loaded rate. Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading – the tool adds it automatically. For more details, see the [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) topic.

## Putting It All Together

To summarise, converting a **business analyst salary in Melbourne** from hourly to annual involves:

1. **Know your hourly rate** – whether it's the base rate or includes casual loading.
2. **Assume 38 hours per week** unless your award specifies different ordinary hours.
3. **Multiply by 52 weeks** to get annual gross.
4. **Add super** at 12% on top (not included in the hourly rate).
5. **Estimate tax** using the resident scale and Medicare levy.

Always verify your specific award or agreement using the Fair Work Ombudsman's [pay guides](/blog) or the Fair Work Commission's database. The [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page provides the latest legal minimums.

Remember, this is an estimate. Your actual pay may vary due to overtime, allowances, salary sacrifice, or enterprise agreements. Use the tools on this site to get a personalised calculation.
